title: Australian parrots and their adaptation to habitat change
sourceHeading: Australian Parrots and Their Adaptation to Habitat Change

source.filename: Practice 170 - IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 2.pdf

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Parrots are found throughout the tropics and on every Southern Hemisphere continent except Antarctica, but nowhere do they display such richness of diversity and form as in Australia. One-sixth of the world’s 345 parrot species are found there, and Australia has long been renowned for the number and variety of its parrots.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the sixteenth century, the German cartographer Mercator made a world map that included a place near present-day Australia which he named Terra Psittacorum—the Land of Parrots—and the first European settlers in Australia often referred to the country as Parrot Land. In 1865, the celebrated British naturalist and wildlife artist John Gould said, ‘No group of birds gives Australia so tropical and benign an air as the numerous species of this great family by which it is tenanted.’

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Parrots descend from an ancient line. Given their great diversity and the fact that most species inhabit Africa, Australia and South America, it seems almost certain that parrots originated millions of years ago on the ancient southern continent of Gondwana, before it broke up into the separate Southern Hemisphere continents we know today. Much of Gondwana comprised vast rainforests intersected by huge, slow-flowing rivers and expansive lakes, but by eight million years ago great changes were under way. The centre of Australia had begun to dry out, and the rainforests that once covered it gradually contracted to the continental margins, where they still exist to a limited extent today.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The creatures that remained in those shrinking rainforests had to adapt to drier conditions or face extinction. Reacting to these desperate circumstances, the parrot family—typically found in jungles elsewhere in the world—populated some of Australia’s harshest environments. Parrots spread from ancestral forests through eucalypt woodlands to colonise the central deserts of Australia. Consequently, they diversified into a wide range of species whose adaptations reflect the many changes animals and plants had to make to survive in these areas.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These evolutionary pressures helped mould keratin, the substance from which beaks are made, into a range of tools capable of gathering the new food types favoured by different parrot species. The size of a parrot’s short, blunt beak and the length of its curved upper section are related to the food the species eats. Some have comparatively long beaks that are perfect for extracting seeds from fruit; others have broader, stronger beaks designed to crack hard seeds.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Differently shaped beaks are not the only adaptations produced during the developing relationship between parrots and their food plants. Like all of Australia’s many honey-eating birds, rainbow-coloured lorikeets and the flowers on which they feed have long co-evolved. Features such as the flowers’ shape and colour have adapted to the birds’ needs. For example, red is particularly attractive to birds, so flowers that depend on birds for pollination are often red, while lorikeets’ tongues have bristles that help them collect as much pollen as possible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Today, most Australian parrots inhabit woodland and open forest, and their numbers decline towards both deserts and wetter areas. Most are nomadic to some degree, moving to take advantage of feeding and breeding sites. Two dry-country parrots—the pink-and-grey galah and the pink, white and yellow corella—have expanded their ranges in recent years. They are among the species that have adapted well to changes brought about by European settlement: forest felling created grasslands where galahs and corellas thrive.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Other parrot species did not fare so well when their environments were altered. The clearing of large areas of rainforest is probably responsible for the disappearance of the double-eyed fig parrot, while ground-parrot numbers declined after much of their habitat was destroyed by the draining of coastal swamps. Even some species that initially benefited from forest clearing now face a shortage of nesting sites because of further human-made changes.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: New conditions sometimes favour an incoming species over one that originally inhabited the area. After farmers cleared large areas of forest on Kangaroo Island, off the coast of South Australia, for example, galahs colonised the island. They soon entered nesting holes and destroyed black-cockatoo eggs so that they could occupy the holes themselves. Their success precipitated a partial collapse in the black-cockatoo population when the latter lost the struggle for scarce nesting hollows.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: There may be no final answer to ensuring an equitable balance among parrot species. Nest-box programmes help ease the shortage of nesting sites in some places, but there are too few of them; they are expensive and no adequate substitute for large, old trees, which provide both habitat and nectar, pollen and seeds. Competition among parrots for nesting sites results from the changes humans have made to the Earth. We are the most widespread and dangerous competitors parrots have ever faced, but we also have the knowledge and skill to maintain Australia’s wonderfully rich diversity of parrots. All we need is the will to do so.

Questions 15–20
Reading Passage 2 has ten paragraphs, A–J.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–J, in boxes 15–20 on your answer sheet.
15 __________ An example of one parrot species surviving at the expense of another
16 __________ A description of how plants may adapt to attract birds
17 __________ Examples of two parrot species that benefited from environmental change
18 __________ How Australia’s varied landscape produced a great variety of parrot species
19 __________ A reason why most parrot species are native to the Southern Hemisphere

Questions 21–23
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 21–23 on your answer sheet.


21 The writer believes that most parrot species
  A moved from Africa and South America to Australia.
  B had ancestors in either Africa, Australia or South America.
  C had ancestors on a continent that later split apart.
  D came from a continent now covered by water.


22 What does the writer say about parrots’ beaks?
  A They are longer than those of other birds.
  B They are made from a unique material.
  C They are used more efficiently than those of other species.
  D They are specially adapted to suit the birds’ diets.


23 Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a disadvantage of nesting boxes?
  A They are too expensive.
  B They need to be maintained.
  C They provide shelter but not food.
  D There are too few of them.

Questions 24–27
